PART I. CLINICAL CHEMISTRY: INSTRUMENTATION

1. Basic concepts of light and photometry

Photometry is the measurement of light. Light is a form of energy that travels in waves; wavelength is expressed in nanometers (nm).

TermDefinition
Peak / crestHighest point of a light wave
TroughLowest point of a light wave
WavelengthDistance between two successive peaks
PhotodetectorConverts light energy into electrical energy

Must memorize: Wavelength and energy are inversely proportional: shorter wavelength = higher energy; longer wavelength = lower energy.

RegionWavelength range in the reviewerKey point
Ultraviolet (UV)4–400 nmHigher energy
Visible light400–700 nmDetectable by the human eye
Infrared (IR)700 nm–0.3 cmLower energy

The reviewer notes that some reference texts use different UV boundaries; retain the range stated in the MTAP material for this assessment.

Types of photometric principles

MethodWhat is measured?Memory clue
SpectrophotometryAbsorbed lightAbsorption
Atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS)Light absorbed by free ground-state atomsAtomic absorption
Flame emission photometryEmitted lightEmission
FluorometryFluorescent light emitted after excitationFluorescence
NephelometryScattered light, commonly detected at an angle to the incident beamScattering
TurbidimetryDecrease in transmitted light caused by suspended particlesCloudiness
Reflectance photometryReflected lightReflection

Do not confuse: Nephelometry measures what is scattered. Turbidimetry measures what fails to pass through. Nephelometry can be used to measure immunoglobulins and other proteins through antigen–antibody complexes; turbidimetry measures turbidity through reduced light transmission. Reflectance photometry is used by automated urine dipstick readers.

2. Beer–Lambert law and spectrophotometer

The Beer–Lambert law describes the relationship between absorbance and concentration.

A = a × b × cA = absorbance · a = absorptivity coefficient · b = path length · c = concentration

When absorptivity and path length are constant, A ∝ C. Increased concentration produces increased absorbance. Higher absorbance means lower transmittance under the same optical conditions.

A = 2 − log(%T)Relationship between absorbance and percentage transmittance.

For an unknown and a standard under the same conditions:

Au / As = Cu / CsAu = absorbance of unknown · As = absorbance of standard · Cu = concentration of unknown · Cs = concentration of standard

Worked example: Unknown absorbance = 0.20; standard absorbance = 0.80; standard concentration = 100 mg/dL. Therefore, 0.20/0.80 = x/100, so x = 25 mg/dL.

OrderComponentFunction / key detail
1Light sourceProvides radiant energy. Tungsten-halogen/iodide is used for visible and IR; UV sources include deuterium, xenon-arc, and mercury-arc lamps.
2MonochromatorSelects or isolates a specific wavelength; may use a prism, diffraction grating, or interference filter.
3Cuvette / sample holderHolds the sample; must be transparent and free of scratches. The lecture notes square-ended cuvettes help maintain equal side thicknesses.
4DetectorConverts light energy into electrical energy; examples include barrier-layer cells, photodiodes, and photomultiplier tubes.
5Readout systemDisplays the measured signal; examples include digital displays, ammeters, and galvanometers.

High yield: The photomultiplier tube (PMT) is the most sensitive detector.

Exam trap: The Caraway method measures the colored tungsten-blue product. The enzymatic uric acid method monitors uric acid by UV absorbance. At 340 nm, NADH absorbs strongly, while NAD⁺ has much less absorbance.

PART II. QUALITY ASSURANCE AND QUALITY CONTROL

1. Basic definitions and the three phases of testing

TermDefinitionMain purpose

Exam trap: QA covers the entire testing process; QC primarily monitors the analytical phase. Accreditation applies to institutions/programs, not individuals; individuals are licensed or certified.

2. Preanalytical considerations and specimen collection

Fasting is commonly required for selected tests; plain water is generally permitted. Not every laboratory procedure requires fasting.

Collection time matters: cortisol is higher in the morning (approximately 6–8 AM) and lower in the afternoon; growth hormone may increase in the afternoon and during deep sleep.

For therapeutic drug monitoring, timing depends on the dosing schedule and whether a peak or trough is requested.

Memory aid: Blood culture → citrate → serum → heparin → EDTA → fluoride. For anticoagulant tubes: CHEF (Citrate, Heparin, EDTA, Fluoride).

PART III. CARBOHYDRATES AND GLUCOSE

1. Characteristics, classification, digestion, and metabolism

Carbohydrates are composed primarily of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Most are water-soluble and most are reducing sugars. Sucrose is the important non-reducing disaccharide.

ClassificationExamplesImportant detail
MonosaccharidesGlucose, fructose, galactoseSimplest carbohydrate units
DisaccharidesLactose, sucrose, maltoseTwo monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond
PolysaccharidesGlycogen, starch, chitinLong chains of sugar units

GlucoseMonosaccharideYesMain circulating blood sugar
FructoseMonosaccharideYesExcess may cause GI symptoms in malabsorption
GalactoseMonosaccharideYesComponent of lactose
LactoseDisaccharideYesGlucose + galactose; lactose intolerance reflects lactase deficiency
MaltoseDisaccharideYesGlucose + glucose

The reviewer identifies absorption through the duodenum and ileum. In humans, the principal storage form of glucose is glycogen.

Hormonal regulation of glucose

HormoneSourceEffect on blood glucose
InsulinPancreatic beta cellsDecreases glucose; increases cellular uptake, glycogenesis, and lipogenesis
GlucagonPancreatic alpha cellsIncreases glucose
EpinephrineAdrenal medullaIncreases glucose
CortisolAdrenal cortexIncreases glucose
Growth hormoneAnterior pituitaryIncreases glucose

2. Specimen collection and preservation for glucose

Specimens identified in the reviewer: whole blood, serum, plasma, CSF, serous fluids, synovial fluid, and urine.

Blood cells continue consuming glucose after collection (glycolysis), causing glucose concentration to decrease if processing is delayed.

Sodium fluoride (NaF) is an antiglycolytic agent. It inhibits enolase by interfering with magnesium-dependent glycolysis; the lecture concentration is 2 mg/mL of whole blood.

Fluoride is a weak anticoagulant and is commonly combined with an anticoagulant such as potassium oxalate in gray-top tubes. The lecture notes that fluoride can inhibit glycolysis for approximately 48–72 hours.

CSF glucose is approximately 60–70% of plasma glucose. Blood glucose should ideally be collected approximately 1–2 hours before lumbar puncture for comparison.

3. Methods of glucose determination

MethodTypeReagent / enzymePositive reaction or measured substanceWavelength / detail
Folin–WuChemicalPhosphomolybdateBlueNot specified in the lecture
Nelson–SomogyiChemicalArsenomolybdateBlueNot specified in the lecture
NeocuproineChemicalNeocuproineYellow to yellow-orangeNot specified in the lecture
Hagedorn–JensenChemicalFerric reagentFe³⁺ reduced to Fe²⁺Ferric reduction method
Dubowski / o-toluidineChemicalo-Toluidine + acetic acidBluish-green complex620–630 nm; heat at approximately 100°C
Glucose oxidaseEnzymaticGlucose oxidase; peroxidase in colorimetric approachOxygen depletion or color formationMethod-dependent
Hexokinase–G6PDEnzymaticHexokinase + glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenaseNADH formation340 nm; reference method in the reviewer

Chemical versus enzymatic: Copper-reduction methods reduce cupric ions (Cu²⁺) to cuprous ions (Cu⁺). They detect reducing substances, not glucose exclusively, and do not detect non-reducing sucrose. The ferric-reduction method is also called Hagedorn–Jensen. Dubowski is a chemical method, not an enzymatic method.

Glucose oxidase detects beta-D-glucose. Mutarotase converts alpha-glucose into beta-glucose; without adequate conversion, glucose oxidase alone may underestimate glucose. The lecture lists beta-glucose at approximately 65% and alpha-glucose at approximately 35%.

The hexokinase–G6PD method is the preferred highly specific enzymatic method in the reviewer: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) + ADP; then G6P + NAD⁺ → 6-phosphogluconate + NADH + H⁺. The NADH is measured at 340 nm. Hexokinase alone is not glucose-specific; the second G6PD reaction provides analytical specificity.

Glucose tests and clinical applications

TestCollection / measurementClinical application
Random blood glucoseAny time of dayEmergency evaluation of hypo- or hyperglycemia
Fasting blood glucose (FBS)After 8–10 hours fasting in the lectureBaseline glucose assessment
2-hour postprandial glucoseTwo hours after eatingPost-meal glucose control

Oral glucose challenge test (OGCT)50 g glucose load, followed by testingScreening for gestational diabetes

Exam alert: HbA1c is affected by RBC lifespan, not only glucose concentration. A single elevated fasting glucose result should not automatically be treated as definitive confirmation of diabetes in an asymptomatic patient.

PART IV. LIPIDS AND LIPOPROTEINS

1. Characteristics and classification of lipids

Lipids are organic substances composed mainly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Their major property is water-insolubility.

Lipid classCompositionMain function / association
Triglycerides (TAG)Three fatty acids + one glycerolEnergy storage; thermal insulation and shock absorption
CholesterolSterol structure; approximately 70% esterified and 30% free in the lectureCell membranes; precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D
PhospholipidsGlycerol + two fatty acids + phosphate-containing groupAmphipathic cell-membrane structure
Fatty acidsHydrocarbon chain with terminal carboxyl groupBuilding blocks of lipids

Phospholipids contain a hydrophilic (polar) region and a hydrophobic (nonpolar) region. Examples in the reviewer include phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine, and lysophosphatidylcholine.

2. Lipoproteins and apolipoproteins

Lipoproteins are complexes of lipids and proteins that transport hydrophobic lipids through blood.

LipoproteinMain functionMain origin / pathwayMain lipid transported
ChylomicronsTransport dietary / exogenous TAGIntestineTriglycerides
VLDLTransport endogenous TAGLiverTriglycerides
IDLIntermediate between VLDL and LDLVLDL metabolismTAG and cholesterol
LDLDelivers cholesterol to peripheral cellsVLDL / IDL metabolismCholesterol
HDLReverse cholesterol transportLiver and intestineCholesterol

Density, lowest to highest: chylomicron → VLDL → IDL → LDL → HDL. Size, largest to smallest, follows the same order. Chylomicrons are the largest and least dense; HDL is the smallest and most dense.

ApolipoproteinFound inMain function / examination clue
Apo A-IHDLActivates LCAT
Apo A-IIHDLMay inhibit lipoprotein and hepatic lipases
Apo A-IVHDL, chylomicrons, free plasmaMay act as LCAT cofactor; increases with fat absorption
Apo B-100VLDL, LDLStructural protein; synthesized in liver
Apo B-48ChylomicronsStructural protein synthesized in intestine
Apo C-IChylomicrons, VLDLMay inhibit hepatic uptake of VLDL and cholesteryl ester transfer protein
Apo C-IIChylomicrons, VLDLActivates lipoprotein lipase (LPL)
Apo C-IIIVLDL, HDLInhibits lipolysis and delays clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins
Apo (a)Lp(a)Homologous to plasminogen; associated with prothrombotic risk
EnzymeFunction
LCATLecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase; esterifies free cholesterol in plasma.
Lipoprotein lipase (LPL)Hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL.
Hepatic lipaseHelps metabolize remnants and HDL / IDL particles.

Frequently tested: Apo A-I → LCAT; Apo C-II → LPL; Apo B-100 → LDL/VLDL structure; Apo B-48 → chylomicron structure; Apo C-III → inhibits lipolysis.

Lipoprotein composition and abnormal lipoproteins

Most triglyceride-rich: chylomicrons. Most protein-rich: HDL. Most cholesterol-rich: LDL.

Electrophoresis separates lipoproteins according to electrical charge/mobility; ultracentrifugation separates by density.

HDL separation may use heparan sulfate–Mn²⁺, dextran sulfate–MgCl₂, phosphotungstate–MgCl₂, or heparin–Ca²⁺. Selected lipoproteins are precipitated, permitting HDL measurement in the supernatant.

Beta-VLDL is associated with Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia. Lp(a) is associated with premature atherosclerosis. LpX is associated with obstructive biliary disease / cholestasis.

3. Triglyceride and cholesterol determination

MethodKey sequence / reagentsPositive reaction / measurement
Van Handel–Zilversmit / Hantzsch (chemical TAG)TAG hydrolysis → glycerol + fatty acids; glycerol oxidation → formaldehyde; chromogenic reactionMeasured component is glycerol; chromotropic acid + sulfuric acid or acetyl acetone + ammonia
Enzymatic TAGLipase → glycerol; glycerol kinase → glycerol-3-phosphate; glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase → dihydroxyacetone phosphate; diaphoraseFormazan, quinoneimine dye, or NADH/NAD⁺ change depending on the coupled system
Chemical cholesterolExamples: Zlatkis, Zak and Boyle; Liebermann–Burchard; Salkowski; Carr and Drekter; Abell–Kendall; Schoenheimer/SperryLiebermann–Burchard: green; approximately 410 nm stated in the lecture
Enzymatic cholesterolCholesterol esterase → cholesterol oxidase → peroxidaseColored product from H₂O₂ and chromogen

Enzyme order: For triglyceride determination, the commonly tested sequence is lipase → glycerol kinase → glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase → diaphorase. The measured component is glycerol generated from TAG, not fatty acids.

For the enzymatic cholesterol method: (1) cholesterol esterase releases free cholesterol from cholesteryl esters; (2) cholesterol oxidase acts on free cholesterol and generates hydrogen peroxide; (3) peroxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize a chromogen. Memorize esterase → oxidase → peroxidase.

IISaponificationAlcoholic KOH splits cholesterol esters

MethodPositive reaction / lecture detail
Liebermann–BurchardGreen; approximately 410 nm in the lecture
SalkowskiColor reaction involving cholesterol and sulfuric acid
Zlatkis, Zak and BoyleChemical colorimetric cholesterol method

Specimen considerations for lipid analysis

The lecture specifies serum or EDTA plasma for cholesterol and triglycerides.

The lecture instructions state fasting for at least 12 hours for lipid testing; current laboratory protocols may not require fasting for every routine lipid profile, so follow the validated procedure and physician request.

Avoid hemolyzed samples, icteric samples when the method is affected, and water contamination.

PART V. PROTEINS AND SERUM PROTEIN ELECTROPHORESIS

1. Protein characteristics and functions

Proteins are composed of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen. Nitrogen distinguishes proteins from the other major macromolecules. Their basic structural units are amino acids. Proteins are amphoteric and can act as acids or bases depending on pH.

Most serum proteins are synthesized by the liver, except immunoglobulins, which are produced by plasma cells. Serum proteins are expressed in g/dL; CSF protein is expressed in mg/dL and is much lower than serum/plasma protein concentration.

2. Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP)

Electrophoresis separates molecules according to electrical charge and mobility in an electric field. At alkaline pH 8.6, most serum proteins acquire a net negative charge and migrate toward the anode (+). Albumin migrates fastest toward the anode.

FeatureImportant fact
Support mediaAgarose gel, cellulose acetate, paper, or polyacrylamide
Common pH8.6
Positive electrodeAnode
Negative electrodeCathode
StainsCoomassie Brilliant Blue, Amido Black, Ponceau S
QuantitationDensitometer

BetaTransferrin, beta-lipoproteins, fibrinogen (in plasma), complement
Alpha-2Alpha-2 macroglobulin, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, hemopexin
Alpha-1Alpha-1 antitrypsin, alpha-1 acid glycoprotein, alpha-fetoprotein
AlbuminAlbumin; fastest toward the anode

The reviewer gives the sequence from the origin toward the anode as γ → β → α₂ → α₁ → albumin.

Beta–gamma bridgingBeta and gamma fractions become connectedLiver cirrhosis
Monoclonal spikeSharp, narrow spike in gamma regionMonoclonal gammopathy, e.g. multiple myeloma
Increased alpha-1 and alpha-2Increased acute-phase proteinsAcute inflammation
Decreased albumin, increased alpha-2Albumin loss and compensatory increase in alpha-2 macroglobulinNephrotic syndrome
Decreased alpha-1Reduced alpha-1 antitrypsinEmphysema associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

Exam trap: Fibrinogen is present in plasma, not properly clotted serum. Fibrinogen may create an additional beta-region band when plasma is used.

PART VI. ENZYMES AND CLINICAL ENZYMOLOGY

1. Characteristics, activity units, and reaction kinetics

Enzymes are biological catalysts that decrease the activation energy required for biochemical reactions. They increase reaction rate, are not consumed, and are generally proteins (although some RNA molecules also have catalytic activity). Enzyme activity is measured rather than simply enzyme quantity.

E + S ⇌ ES → E + PEnzyme + substrate ⇌ enzyme–substrate complex → enzyme + product
UnitDefinition
International unit (IU or U)Amount of enzyme that converts 1 micromole of substrate per minute.
Katal (kat)Amount of enzyme that converts 1 mole of substrate per second.
FactorEffect on enzymatic reactions
TemperatureChanges reaction velocity; excessive heat denatures enzymes.
pHAlters enzyme structure and active-site ionization.
Enzyme concentrationHigher concentration generally increases reaction rate if substrate is sufficient.
Substrate concentrationIncreases reaction rate until saturation.
InhibitorsDecrease enzyme activity.
Activators / cofactorsSupport enzyme activity.

The lecture describes the Q₁₀ temperature coefficient as an approximate doubling of reaction rate for every 10°C increase; this is an approximation, not a universal rule for all temperatures and enzymes.

TermDefinition
VmaxMaximum reaction velocity.
KmSubstrate concentration at half Vmax.
Enzyme saturationCondition where most active sites are occupied.
Zero-order kineticsAt sufficiently high substrate concentration, velocity is independent of substrate concentration and proportional to enzyme concentration.
First-order kineticsReaction velocity depends on substrate concentration.

Clinical enzyme assays are commonly performed under zero-order conditions: sufficiently high substrate concentration saturates the enzyme so that reaction rate is proportional to enzyme concentration.

2. Related enzyme terms, cofactors, and classification

Holoenzyme = Apoenzyme + CofactorComplete active enzyme = protein component + required non-protein component
TermDefinition / example

PART VII. LIVER FUNCTION TESTS AND BILIRUBIN

1. Liver functions and liver function tests

The liver is one of the largest and most metabolically versatile organs. The lecture gives an approximate weight of 1.4–1.6 kg and identifies the hepatic lobule as the smallest functional unit.

FunctionExplanation / laboratory correlate
SyntheticProduces albumin, clotting factors, and other proteins; assess albumin, total protein, and PT/INR.
DetoxificationMetabolizes drugs, toxins, and hormones; ammonia is relevant to hepatic dysfunction.
ExcretoryExcretes bilirubin and other substances through bile; assess bilirubin.
MetabolicRegulates carbohydrate, protein, and lipid metabolism.
Hepatocellular injuryALT and AST.
Hepatobiliary / cholestatic injuryALP and GGT.

Important distinction: Liver enzymes are primarily markers of injury, not direct measurements of liver synthetic capacity.

2. Bilirubin metabolism and B1 versus B2

Hemoglobin is broken down; heme is converted to biliverdin, then to unconjugated bilirubin.

Unconjugated bilirubin travels bound to albumin and is taken up by hepatocytes.

UDP-glucuronyl transferase conjugates bilirubin. Conjugated bilirubin enters bile.

Intestinal bacteria convert bilirubin into urobilinogen. Some urobilinogen is reabsorbed and some is excreted.

CharacteristicBilirubin I (B1)Bilirubin II (B2)
Other nameHemobilirubinCholebilirubin
TypeUnconjugated / indirectConjugated / direct
PolarityNonpolarPolar
Water solubilityInsolubleSoluble
Albumin bindingStrongly boundLess strongly bound
UrineNot normally excretedCan be excreted

3. Hyperbilirubinemia: prehepatic, hepatic, and posthepatic

FindingPrehepaticHepaticPosthepatic
Main problemExcess bilirubin productionHepatocyte dysfunctionBiliary obstruction
Typical associationHemolytic anemiaHepatitis / liver diseaseObstructive jaundice
Serum B1IncreasedIncreasedUsually not predominant
Serum B2Not predominantly increasedIncreasedIncreased
Urine bilirubinNegativePositivePositive
Urine urobilinogenIncreasedIncreasedDecreased

Prehepatic: excess RBC destruction produces more unconjugated bilirubin than the liver can process. Hepatic: the liver cannot efficiently process and/or excrete bilirubin. Posthepatic: conjugated bilirubin cannot flow normally into the intestine, refluxes into blood, and appears in urine; less bilirubin reaches the intestine, so urobilinogen decreases.

PART VIII. ACID–BASE BALANCE AND BLOOD GAS ANALYSIS

1. Goal of acid–base balance and Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

Normal arterial pH: 7.35–7.45. Below 7.35 = acidemia; above 7.45 = alkalemia.

OrganMain role
LungsRegulate carbon dioxide (CO₂).
KidneysRegulate bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) and hydrogen-ion excretion.
pH = 6.1 + log [HCO₃⁻ / (0.03 × pCO₂)]Bicarbonate is directly proportional to pH; pCO₂ is inversely proportional to pH.

The bicarbonate-to-carbonic acid ratio is approximately 20:1. The phosphate buffer ratio in the lecture is 4:1.

Buffer systemComponentsImportant function
Bicarbonate–carbonic acidHCO₃⁻ / H₂CO₃Major extracellular buffer
PhosphateHPO₄²⁻ / H₂PO₄⁻Important intracellular and renal buffer
HemoglobinHemoglobin and proton-binding formsBuffers hydrogen ions in RBCs
Plasma proteinsAlbumin and other proteinsAmphoteric buffering

Oxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to oxygen; carbaminohemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon dioxide; carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide.

Exam trap: Carbaminohemoglobin is not carboxyhemoglobin.

1. Check pH: acidosis or alkalosis?

2. Check pCO₂: does it explain the pH change?

3. Check HCO₃⁻: does it explain the pH change?

4. Identify the primary disorder.

5. Determine whether compensation is present.

6. Evaluate the anion gap when metabolic acidosis is present.

AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)Potassium is excluded in the common reference range given here.
Anion gapInterpretation / associations
IncreasedAccumulation of unmeasured anions; may be associated with lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, renal failure, toxic alcohols, and salicylates.
NormalOften associated with bicarbonate loss and compensatory chloride retention.

Preferred specimen: Heparinized arterial whole blood, collected in a heparinized blood gas syringe. Ordinary Vacutainer tubes are not the preferred specimen container for blood gas analysis.

Requirement / problemReason / effect
Seal syringe with rubber stopperPrevents exposure to atmospheric air.
Place in ice bath if delayed (per lecture)Slows cellular metabolism.
Avoid clots and hemolysisPrevents inaccurate measurement and specimen interference.

Delay in analysis of sealed whole bloodpO₂ decreases, pCO₂ increases, and pH decreases.

Room air contains approximately 21% oxygen. Blood cells continue cellular respiration after collection, consuming oxygen and producing carbon dioxide; increased CO₂ raises carbonic acid and decreases pH.

Memory clue: Glass = pH; Severinghaus = pCO₂; Clark = pO₂. Potentiometry measures pH and pCO₂; amperometry measures pO₂.

PART IX. NON-PROTEIN NITROGEN COMPOUNDS (NPNS)

1. General characteristics of non-protein nitrogen compounds

NPNs are nitrogen-containing compounds that are not proteins. The reviewer lists urea, amino acids, uric acid, creatinine, creatine, and ammonia. Urea is the most predominant NPN (approximately 45% in the lecture); amino acids are second most predominant.

CompoundMajor clinical application
Urea / BUNKidney function
Uric acidPurine metabolism and gout
CreatinineKidney function
AmmoniaLiver function and hepatic encephalopathy

2. Urea, BUN, and methods of determination

Urea is the major end product of protein metabolism. It is produced in the liver through the urea cycle, excreted by the kidneys, and partially reabsorbed in the renal tubules.

CharacteristicUreaBUN
What is measured?Entire urea moleculeNitrogen component of urea
Chemical formulaNH₂CONH₂Nitrogen portion of urea
Unitsmg/dLmg/dL
RelationshipLarger numerical valueSmaller numerical value
Urea = BUN × 2.14BUN = Urea × 0.4673

Example from the reviewer: BUN = 20 mg/dL → urea = 20 × 2.14 = 42.8 mg/dL.

MethodReagent / principlePositive result or measurement

o-Phthaldehydeo-PhthaldehydeMethod-dependent colored reaction

In the coupled enzymatic method, urease acts first, converting urea to ammonia/ammonium and carbon dioxide. Glutamate dehydrogenase then uses ammonia with alpha-ketoglutarate and NADH; NADH is consumed and absorbance change is monitored at 340 nm.

Do not confuse: Azotemia is a biochemical finding (increased nitrogen-containing waste products in blood); uremia is a clinical syndrome associated with accumulation of uremic toxins and organ involvement.

3. Uric acid, creatinine, and ammonia

Uric acid

Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism in humans, produced primarily in the liver and excreted through the kidneys. It is filtered and substantially reabsorbed in renal tubules and acts as a reducing agent.

MethodReagent / principlePositive reaction / wavelength
Caraway / Henry chemical methodPhosphotungstic acidTungsten blue; 650–700 nm, approximately 660 nm
Enzymatic uricase methodUricase oxidizes uric acid to allantoin, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen peroxideUV at 293 nm, colorimetric method, or coupled peroxidase method

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is caused by HGPRT deficiency, impairing the purine salvage pathway and increasing uric acid production. The classic examination clue in the reviewer is orange sand-like crystals in the diaper.

Creatinine

Creatinine is the end product of muscle creatine metabolism. It is produced at a relatively constant rate in an individual, largely according to muscle mass; it is freely filtered at the glomerulus, not significantly reabsorbed, and a small amount is secreted by renal tubules. The reviewer identifies it as the preferred routine endogenous marker among the NPNs for assessing renal filtration.

MethodReagent / principleImportant detail
Jaffe reactionAlkaline picrate (picric acid + sodium hydroxide)Orange-red colored complex; endpoint and kinetic approaches
Endpoint JaffeSimplest methodMore susceptible to interference
Kinetic JaffeKinetic measurementPreferred in the lecture; better control of nonspecific interference
Enzymatic methodsCreatinine aminohydrolase–creatine kinase or creatininase–hydrogen peroxideEnzymatic conversion / coupled hydrogen peroxide measurement

Fuller’s earth and Lloyd’s reagent are listed as adsorbents for removing interfering substances. Increased creatinine may result from reduced kidney function, increased muscle mass, increased creatine turnover, muscle injury, or increased muscle metabolism.

Ammonia

Ammonia is an immediate product of amino acid deamination. Sources include dietary protein breakdown, intestinal bacterial/enzymatic metabolism, and urea hydrolysis. The lecture identifies the small intestine as the primary production site.

Ammonia is toxic, especially to the CNS. The liver detoxifies it by converting it into urea through the urea cycle. The Berthelot method uses sodium hypochlorite + phenol to produce indophenol blue. Other methods include Conway microdiffusion, ion-exchange, coupled enzymatic measurement, and an ion-selective electrode.

In the coupled enzymatic method, glutamate dehydrogenase is important; NADH is consumed and absorbance change is measured at 340 nm. The reviewer cautions that urease is used for urea measurement, not as the second enzyme in the ammonia method.

Ammonia preanalytical errorWhy it matters
Delayed separation / processingAmmonia is highly vulnerable to preanalytical change.
HemolysisCan interfere with measurement.
Ammonium-containing detergentsCan contaminate specimens; disposable test tubes help prevent contamination.
Smoking exposureBoth patient and medical technologist should avoid exposure.

PART X. ELECTROLYTES

1. General characteristics and major electrolytes

Electrolytes dissociate into electrically charged particles in solution. A cation is positively charged; an anion is negatively charged; a counterion balances another ion’s charge. A zwitterion contains both positive and negative charges (example: an amino acid).

ElectrolyteMajor location / typeMain function
Sodium (Na⁺)Major extracellular cationOsmolality and blood volume
Potassium (K⁺)Major intracellular cationNerve impulses and cardiac contraction
Chloride (Cl⁻)Major extracellular anionElectrical neutrality and acid–base balance
PhosphateMajor intracellular anionEnergy metabolism and buffering
Calcium (Ca²⁺)Mostly stored in boneMuscle contraction, coagulation, and bone structure
Magnesium (Mg²⁺)Mostly intracellular and in boneEnzyme cofactor and neuromuscular function

2. Sodium and potassium

Sodium

Sodium is the major extracellular cation. It maintains extracellular osmolality and blood volume, regulates water balance, and contributes to nerve and muscle function. Regulation involves RAAS, ADH and thirst mechanisms, and renal sodium handling.

StateCauses / associations in the reviewer
HypernatremiaDiabetes insipidus (free-water loss), Cushing syndrome, hyperaldosteronism, water deprivation, and excessive water loss.
HyponatremiaSIADH, mineralocorticoid deficiency, hyperglycemia (water shift into extracellular fluid), renal/GI losses, and excessive water intake.

Methods for sodium: flame emission photometry, atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS), and ion-selective electrode (ISE). ISE is the most commonly used routine method.

Potassium

Potassium is the major intracellular cation. It is important for nerve impulse transmission, resting membrane potential, myocardial contraction, and muscle function.

StateCauses / associations
HyperkalemiaPseudohyperkalemia; hemolysis (release of intracellular potassium); mineralocorticoid deficiency; renal failure; tissue destruction.
HypokalemiaInsulin therapy (intracellular shift), alkalosis, mineralocorticoid excess, vomiting/diarrhea, and diuretics.

Exam trap: Hemolysis commonly causes falsely increased potassium. Hyperkalemia may cause tall peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, and widened QRS in severe cases; hypokalemia may cause flattened T waves, ST depression, and prominent U waves.

3. Chloride and phosphate

Chloride is the major extracellular anion. It maintains electrical neutrality and osmolality and participates in acid–base regulation and the chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon), the exchange of chloride and bicarbonate across the RBC membrane that helps transport CO₂.

ConditionAssociation
HyperchloremiaBicarbonate loss, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, and excessive chloride administration.
HypochloremiaProlonged vomiting, diuretics, metabolic alkalosis, and some cases of DKA.
Chloride methodPrinciple
ISESelective response to chloride ions
Amperometric / coulometric titrationElectrical measurement during chloride titration
Schales and SchalesMercurimetric titration
ColorimetricColor reaction
Sweat chlorideMeasurement of chloride in sweat

Phosphate is a major intracellular anion involved in ATP/energy metabolism, intracellular buffering, bone/teeth mineralization, nucleic-acid structure, and phosphorylation. It is regulated by PTH, vitamin D, FGF23, renal tubular reabsorption, and intestinal absorption.

HormoneEffect on calciumEffect on phosphate
PTHIncreases serum calciumIncreases renal phosphate excretion, decreasing serum phosphate
Vitamin DIncreases calcium absorptionIncreases phosphate absorption
CalcitoninDecreases osteoclastic bone resorptionHelps regulate bone mineral metabolism
FGF23Indirect effects on calcium / vitamin DIncreases renal phosphate excretion

Hyperphosphatemia may be associated with renal failure, increased cellular breakdown, intensive exercise, increased intake in susceptible patients, and hypoparathyroidism. Hypophosphatemia may occur with poor intake, vomiting, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, or intracellular phosphate shifts.

Method to memorize: Fiske–Subbarow = phosphate. Phosphate forms a phosphomolybdate complex; reduction produces a blue molybdenum-blue complex.

PART XI. ENDOCRINOLOGY

1. Endocrine system and hormone classification

The endocrine system consists of glands and specialized organs that produce hormones regulating growth, metabolism, reproduction, fluid/electrolyte balance, stress response, and blood glucose.

Feedback mechanismDefinitionExample
Negative feedbackIncreased end product inhibits further productionThyroid hormone suppresses TRH and TSH
Positive feedbackResponse amplifies the original stimulusOxytocin during labor

TSH, LH, FSH, and hCG are glycoprotein hormones. They have similar alpha subunits but different beta subunits; the beta subunit determines biological specificity.

The pituitary is called the master gland because its hormones regulate several other endocrine glands. The posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones produced in the hypothalamus.

Posterior pituitary hormones and water balance

ADH (vasopressin) is produced by the hypothalamus, stored and released by the posterior pituitary, and acts primarily on the kidneys to promote water reabsorption. Increased plasma osmolality stimulates ADH. ADH deficiency or renal resistance can cause diabetes insipidus.

hCGIncreased
Inhibin AIncreased

Must memorize: Down syndrome quadruple marker pattern = two decreased and two increased: AFP ↓, uE3 ↓, hCG ↑, inhibin A ↑. hCG is produced by placental syncytiotrophoblasts; it is used in pregnancy testing and may also be associated with choriocarcinoma and hydatidiform mole.

PART XII. THERAPEUTIC DRUG MONITORING (TDM)

1. Basic concepts, routes, and specimen collection

Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) measures drug concentrations in biological specimens to ensure effective treatment while minimizing toxicity.

TermDefinition
ED50Effective dose in 50% of the population
TD50Toxic dose in 50% of the population
LD50Lethal dose in 50% of the population
First-pass metabolismHepatic metabolism of an orally administered drug before it reaches systemic circulation
RouteImportant characteristic
OralMost common; subject to first-pass metabolism
Intravenous100% bioavailability
IntramuscularAbsorbed from muscle
SubcutaneousAbsorbed from subcutaneous tissue
TranscutaneousThrough tissues / skin
RectalThrough rectal mucosa
SublingualAbsorbed beneath tongue
TransdermalThrough skin

Exam trap: Intravenous administration has 100% bioavailability because the drug enters systemic circulation directly.

Preferred specimens for TDM: serum and heparinized plasma.

Urine is avoided for routine TDM; urine is commonly used for drug-of-abuse testing.

The gel separator in serum separator tubes (SST) can adsorb certain drugs and may produce falsely decreased concentrations.

Include the time of the last dose and the time of specimen collection in the result.

2. Peak versus trough and commonly monitored drugs

FeaturePeak sampleTrough sample
TimingAfter drug administrationImmediately before the next dose
PurposeEvaluates maximum concentrationEvaluates minimum concentration
Lecture timingUsually 30–60 minutes after doseBefore next dose
Important considerationDepends on route and drug absorptionStandardized immediately before next dose
Drug groupExamples / important detail
Cardioactive drugsAmiodarone, digitoxin, digoxin, disopyramide, lidocaine, procainamide, propranolol, quinidine, verapamil.
AnticonvulsantsPhenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, valproic acid, ethosuximide, felbamate, lamotrigine, gabapentin, topiramate.
AntidepressantsAmitriptyline, desipramine, doxepin, imipramine, nortriptyline.
Mood stabilizerLithium: used in bipolar disorder and monitored because of its narrow therapeutic range.
ImmunosuppressantsCyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, leflunomide, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, sirolimus, tacrolimus.
Other monitored groupsAntipsychotics, antineoplastics, bronchodilators (theophylline), anti-inflammatory agents, and antibiotics.

Clinical distinction: Digoxin and digitoxin are both cardiac glycosides, but differ in pharmacokinetics, including elimination.

PART XIII. TOXICOLOGY

1. Ethanol intoxication

The values below are the teaching ranges reproduced in the reviewer, not universal clinical or legal cutoffs. Actual impairment and legal limits depend on jurisdiction and individual circumstances.

Blood alcohol concentration (% w/v)Signs and symptoms
0.01–0.05No obvious impairment; subtle performance changes
0.03–0.12Mild euphoria, decreased inhibitions, some motor impairment
0.09–0.25Loss of critical judgment, memory impairment, diminished reaction time
0.18–0.30Confusion, dizziness, strongly impaired motor skills, staggering, slurred speech
0.27–0.40Unable to stand or walk, vomiting, impaired consciousness
0.35–0.50Coma and possible death
≥0.10The lecture’s stated presumptive evidence of driving under the influence

General progression: euphoria → disinhibition → impaired judgment → confusion → stupor → coma. High concentrations can cause respiratory depression and death.

2. Important toxic substances

Toxic substanceMechanism / sourceImportant clinical clue
OrganophosphatesInsecticides/pesticides; inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing acetylcholine accumulation and cholinergic toxicity.Decreased cholinesterase activity; salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis, miosis, bronchorrhea/bronchospasm, fasciculations, and weakness.
ArsenicEnvironmental / industrial exposure; causes GI, neurologic, cardiovascular, and systemic toxicity.Classic garlic-like odor; chronic exposure can affect skin and peripheral nerves.
CyanideInhibits cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport chain.Classic bitter-almond odor; prevents effective cellular oxygen use and causes histotoxic hypoxia.
Carbon monoxideVehicle exhaust and incomplete combustion; binds hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin.Approximately 200–245 times greater affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen in the lecture; reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and impairs oxygen release. Cherry-red appearance is a traditional clue but not consistently present.
MercuryElemental, mercurous (Hg⁺ / Hg₂²⁺), and mercuric (Hg²⁺) forms.Kidney damage, neurologic toxicity, and GI effects depending on form and exposure.

High yield: Organophosphates = decreased cholinesterase; arsenic = garlic odor; cyanide = bitter almond odor; CO = carboxyhemoglobin; mercury = elemental / mercurous / mercuric.

Other chemistry analytes identified in the reviewer include vitamins and trace elements, drugs of abuse, and tumor markers.

PART XVI. FINAL RAPID-FIRE MEMORY SHEET

1. Final rapid-fire memory sheet

This is the section recommended for immediate pre-examination review. Read the paired terms and high-yield values aloud.

INSTRUMENTATION

  • Visible light = 400–700 nm.
  • Violet = highest energy; red = longest wavelength.
  • Beer–Lambert = A = abc; absorbance is proportional to concentration.
  • PMT = most sensitive detector.
  • Nephelometry = scattered light; turbidimetry = transmitted light blocked.
  • Spectrophotometer order = source → monochromator → cuvette → detector → readout.

QUALITY ASSURANCE

  • QA = entire testing process; QC = analytical phase.
  • Mean = average; median = middle; mode = most frequent.
  • SD = dispersion; CV = relative imprecision.
  • t-test = means; F-test = variances.
  • 1₂s = warning; 1₃s = rejection; 2₂s = systematic; R₄s = random.

CARBOHYDRATES

  • Main circulating sugar = glucose; storage form = glycogen.
  • Non-reducing sugar = sucrose; lactose = glucose + galactose.
  • Dubowski = o-toluidine; positive = bluish-green; 620–630 nm.
  • Glucose oxidase = beta-glucose; mutarotase = alpha to beta glucose.
  • Hexokinase–G6PD = NADH at 340 nm; fluoride inhibits enolase.
  • HbA1c = 2–3 months; fructosamine = 2–3 weeks.
  • Renal glucose threshold = 160–180 mg/dL.

LIPIDS

  • Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids.
  • Cholesterol ester = cholesterol + fatty acid.
  • Phospholipid = glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate.
  • Chylomicrons = exogenous TAG; VLDL = endogenous TAG.
  • LDL = liver-to-cells cholesterol; HDL = reverse cholesterol transport.
  • Apo A-I = LCAT; Apo B-48 = chylomicrons; Apo B-100 = VLDL/LDL.
  • Apo C-II = LPL; Apo C-III = inhibits lipolysis.
  • TAG sequence = lipase → glycerol kinase → GPDH → diaphorase.
  • Cholesterol sequence = esterase → oxidase → peroxidase.
  • Lp(a) = premature atherosclerosis; LpX = obstructive biliary disease.

PROTEINS

  • Nitrogen distinguishes proteins; albumin = oncotic pressure.
  • Transferrin = iron; haptoglobin = hemoglobin; hemopexin = heme.
  • Biuret = peptide bonds, violet at 540 nm; Kjeldahl = nitrogen.
  • SPEP = pH 8.6; albumin migrates fastest toward anode.
  • Beta–gamma bridging = cirrhosis; monoclonal spike = multiple myeloma.

ENZYMES

  • IU = micromole/minute; katal = mole/second.
  • CK-BB = brain; CK-MB = heart; CK-MM = skeletal muscle.
  • Myoglobin is first marker to rise in the lecture’s historical AMI kinetics.
  • ALT = more liver-specific; ALP = bone and liver; GGT = hepatobiliary.
  • Paget disease = increased ALP; lipase = more specific for pancreatitis.
  • Amylase may increase in mumps.
  • RAAS = renin → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II.

LIVER AND BILIRUBIN

  • B1 = unconjugated, indirect, nonpolar; B2 = conjugated, direct, polar.
  • Prehepatic = urine bilirubin negative, urobilinogen increased.
  • Hepatic = urine bilirubin positive, urobilinogen often increased.
  • Posthepatic = urine bilirubin positive, urobilinogen decreased.
  • Gilbert = uptake; Crigler–Najjar = conjugation.
  • Dubin–Johnson = dark liver; Rotor = nonpigmented liver.
  • Van den Bergh = diazo; Jendrassik–Grof = caffeine–sodium benzoate.

NPN

  • Urea = predominant NPN; urea = protein metabolism.
  • Uric acid = purine metabolism; creatinine = muscle metabolism.
  • Ammonia = deamination; BUN × 2.14 = urea.
  • Caraway = uric acid; Jaffe = creatinine; Fearon = diacetyl monoxime.
  • Berthelot = indophenol blue; HGPRT deficiency = Lesch–Nyhan.

ELECTROLYTES AND ACID–BASE

  • Na⁺ = major extracellular cation; K⁺ = major intracellular cation.
  • Cl⁻ = major extracellular anion; phosphate = major intracellular anion.
  • Calcium = bone and coagulation; magnesium = enzyme cofactor.
  • Fiske–Subbarow = phosphate; OCPC = calcium; Calmagite = magnesium; ISE = common electrolyte method.
  • Normal pH = 7.35–7.45; pCO₂ = respiratory; HCO₃⁻ = metabolic.
  • Clark = pO₂; Severinghaus = pCO₂; glass electrode = pH.
  • Potentiometry = pH and pCO₂; amperometry = pO₂.
  • Respiratory acidosis = hypoventilation; respiratory alkalosis = hyperventilation.

ENDOCRINOLOGY

  • Master gland = pituitary; TRH = TSH; CRH = ACTH; GnRH = FSH/LH; GHRH = GH.
  • PIF = prolactin inhibition; GHIH = somatostatin.
  • ADH = water reabsorption; Graves = hyperthyroidism; Hashimoto = hypothyroidism.
  • TBG = main thyroid hormone carrier; GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex.
  • Aldosterone = sodium retention; cortisol = glucocorticoid.
  • VMA = catecholamines; HVA = dopamine; 5-HIAA = serotonin.
  • Insulin = beta cells; glucagon = alpha cells; somatostatin = delta cells.
  • Down syndrome quadruple test = AFP ↓, uE3 ↓, hCG ↑, inhibin A ↑.

TDM AND TOXICOLOGY

  • IV = 100% bioavailability; peak = maximum concentration; trough = before next dose.
  • SST gel can adsorb some drugs.
  • Organophosphates = decreased cholinesterase; arsenic = garlic odor.
  • Cyanide = bitter almond odor; CO = carboxyhemoglobin.
  • Mercury = elemental, mercurous, mercuric.

Final examination priority: Give greatest attention to analytical methods and reagents, enzyme associations, NPN methods, lipoprotein apolipoproteins, bilirubin patterns, and acid–base interpretation. These topics lend themselves to identification, matching, and situational questions.

Reference framework named in the reviewer: Henry’s Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods; Bishop, Fody, and Schoeff’s Clinical Chemistry: Principles, Techniques, and Correlations; and Turgeon’s Clinical Chemistry. These are companion references identified in the PDF, not page-by-page quotations from editions that were not uploaded.
